sources.name: Hamblin TJ
sources.text: "Fake!", BMJ 1981;283(6307):1671-1674 (Christmas issue, 19 Dec 1981): the "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes" framing; the spinach paragraph, including the 1930s German chemists, the "tenfold overestimate", and "chewing the cans"; no citation for the paragraph; the closing list of 13 publications Hamblin "should particularly like to mention". Also indexed on PubMed Central as PMC1507475.

sources.name: Sutton M
sources.text: "Spinach, Iron and Popeye: Ironic lessons from biochemistry and history on the importance of healthy eating, healthy scepticism and adequate citation", Internet Journal of Criminology, 2010. The link is a mirror of the Internet Journal of Criminology paper; the journal's site refuses scripted requests. Supports: Sutton's affiliation (Reader in Criminology, Nottingham Trent University); that none of Hamblin's 13 references cites "the source of the decimal error or 1930's Germans"; Sutton's email exchange with Hamblin, as Sutton reports it ("honestly cannot remember", "asked not to provide references", "sure that he had not made it up"); his conclusion that, "in the absence of references to prove otherwise", Hamblin had invented the decimal error; the dried-spinach figure of 44.8 mg per 100 g (Jackson 1938); Coultate 2009 as quoted, giving von Bunge's 1890 figure of 35 mg per 100 g from dried spinach and the alternative von Wolf decimal version; the strip of 3 July 1932, which Sutton describes as Popeye "explaining for the very first time why he eats spinach", and "Segar chose and promoted spinach for its vitamin A content alone."

sources.name: Rekdal OB
sources.text: "Academic urban legends", Social Studies of Science 2014;44(4):638-654, doi:10.1177/0306312714535679: "In the past 30 years" of retellings as fact; a reader pointing Sutton to Bender, and Sutton's follow-up (Sutton 2010b); Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London ("may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point"); Hamblin "accidentally turned Bender's suggestion into a piece of fact"; Sutton 2010b on "contamination during the analysis or the confusion between fresh and dried spinach"; Hamblin's comment on Sutton 2010b ("I thought it was in Reader's Digest", "very willing to admit that I was wrong"); Kronick 1985 citing Hamblin with "It has been suggested that" and that such phrases "tend to change or disappear"; Larsson 1995, J Intern Med 238(5), "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation", quoted at pp. 448-449, citing Hamblin; "in quite a spectacular way"; the dates 1870, the 1890s and the 1930s; the 5 ways to cite Larsson's sentence, including "I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson"; "doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

sources.name: US Department of Agriculture
sources.text: FoodData Central, "Spinach, raw" (SR Legacy, FDC ID 168462, published 1 April 2019): iron, 2.71 mg per 100 g. The link is the FoodData Central API record, because the site's food pages answer scripted requests with a 404.
